title: What accounts for the 234-359 ms stage-document read?
statement: `readStageDocument` measured 234-359 ms p95 across six runs. It awaits `connection()`, lists the stage directory and reads nine files totalling roughly 90 KB — work that should cost single-digit milliseconds. Which part of that span is actually spending the time, and is it reducible? INSTRUMENT BEFORE OPTIMISING: the three candidates are the `connection()` wait itself, the directory listing plus nine reads, and contention with the sibling `<Suspense>` boundary on the same request — `readStageCriteria` calls `lintProject`, which reads and validates every artifact in the project, concurrently with this read. Nothing has separated them, so all three remain live and none may be assumed.
notes: ⚠️ NON-BLOCKING FOR v1, BY DECISION. The observed 245-375 ms stage response is accepted for a local-first tool on a developer's own machine while the attribution stays open. This is recorded so the unknown stays visible, not so it blocks. ⚠️ IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE FIRST ANSWER WAS WRONG AND CONFIDENT. The span was initially reported as a per-request read of all 253 artifacts. It is not — `lintProject` is not on `readStageDocument`'s path at all. The plausible story was accepted without being measured, which is the same mistake DEC-0020's fallback made about the compiler. Twice now on one measurement, an assumed cause has been wrong; the instruction to instrument before optimising is that pattern being taken seriously. ⚠️ THE CONTENTION HYPOTHESIS IS THE INTERESTING ONE, because if it holds, the cost is not in this read at all — it is the whole-project lint running beside it, and it would move if either boundary changed. It is also the one most easily missed by instrumenting only inside `readStageDocument`. ⚠️ A SEVENTH RUN MEASURED THE READ AT 104.88 ms MEDIAN / 117.12 ms p95 — a THIRD of the 234-359 ms this question was opened about, from the same code against the same content on the same host. The span is not a stable cost, and that is itself the strongest evidence so far: work that is genuinely I/O-bound on nine small files does not vary threefold. It moves the contention hypothesis ahead of the other two, because the thing most likely to differ between runs is what the sibling `<Suspense>` boundary was doing at the time — `readStageCriteria` lints and validates every artifact in the project concurrently with this read. ⚠️ IT ALSO MEANS ACC-0020 WAS DECIDED BY NOISE. Six runs split 3/3 across a 300 ms line while the underlying cost ranged at least 117-359 ms; a seventh run would have passed it. That is the sharpest argument for why the criterion was replaced rather than re-run until it passed. ⚠️ STILL DO NOT OPTIMISE ON THIS. Threefold variance is consistent with contention, with filesystem cache state, and with the `connection()` wait behaving differently under load — the same three candidates, none eliminated. Instrument the three separately first.
